evidence_quotes.quote: An example that was reported by most participants was moving from a position of being self-reliant when using well or spring water to becoming dependent on township water.

Regulations to halt individual, community, or industrial practices that pose risks to our water supply are often stymied by the counterarguments from people who reside within the very communities such regulations are intended to protect.
Two narrative features stemming from our discussions of water took shape as individual and then collective stories transpired; these features transcend time and event particulars.

In this essay, we draw on our experiences as a professor (Jerry) and undergraduate student (David) facilitating focus-group interviews of long-time residents of southeastern Ohio to add their stories to the overall narratives of water use and access.
“We bought the tap three years before. Before the pipe ever got there,” Wilson said.
Through the stories here, I find an acceptance of this liminal space, in which lived experience in opposition to “the Other” defines a community.

criterion_notes.c1: Satisfied. Alongside broader stories about river flooding, agricultural irrigation, fracking attitudes, and C8 river pollution, focus-group participants recount household drinking-water access experiences, specifically transitioning from private wells, springs, and cisterns to township piped water systems, waiting for main-line extension after purchasing a tap, and temporary outage from a frozen meter.
criterion_notes.c2: Not satisfied under either reading. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (c2 = no), the essay does not analyze any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility-governance mechanism governing household water service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, enforcement, or formal connection rules). One participant (Wilson, PDF p. 4) remarks in passing that after buying a tap the water company needed enough sign-ups before laying the line, and another (Jesse, PDF p. 4) recounts a frozen meter dispute, but the paper does not study utility connection rules or administrative governance, using these anecdotes solely to illustrate emotional 'liminality' and 'othering.' References to an Ohio Supreme Court ruling on local fracking bans, DuPont C8 litigation, and Kansas agricultural irrigation wells concern extractive/environmental regulation or farming rather than household service-access rules. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it also fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because the essay's analytical focus is health-communication narrative identity ('liminality' and 'otherness') in living with water and nature rather than examining any legal, institutional, or governance factor governing service access (and even if environmental/utility mentions were construed broadly, c5 fails).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfied at a minimal qualitative level. Although published in Health Communication's autobiographical/reflective 'Defining Moments' rubric interleaving the authors' personal memoirs with participant stories and lacking a formal Methods section, the text reports primary qualitative data in the form of verbatim excerpts from focus-group interviews conducted by the authors with long-time southeastern Ohio residents.
criterion_notes.c4: Satisfied anecdotally. While the authors' main analytical outcomes are narrative themes ('liminality' and 'otherness'), participant accounts describe household connection transitions from wells/springs/cisterns to township water, a three-year wait between buying a tap and pipe installation, and a temporary service interruption from a frozen water meter.
criterion_notes.c5: Not satisfied. As a 4-page 'Defining Moments' reflective essay, the article reports no sample size, number of focus groups, recruitment strategy, interview protocol, or qualitative coding/analytic method, and defines no identifiable governance/legal exposure linked to a service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfied. Full text is in English.

study_design: Reflective narrative essay ('Defining Moments') incorporating qualitative focus-group interview excerpts (formal sampling and analytic methods not reported)
population_and_sample: Long-time residents of southeastern Ohio (Appalachian Ohio region) who worked on or lived near water participating in focus-group interviews (12 named speakers quoted; total sample size and number of focus groups not reported)
exposure: Living with water, environmental uncertainty ('Mother Nature'), industrial/extractive water risks (fracking, C8 river contamination), and shifting from private wells/springs/cisterns to township water (no legal, administrative, or regulatory service-access mechanism examined)
outcome: Health-communication narrative themes of 'liminality' and 'otherness' in community storytelling, alongside anecdotal mentions of transitioning to township water, a 3-year delay in pipe installation after buying a tap, and a frozen meter outage
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). This 4-page 'Defining Moments' reflective essay in Health Communication combines autobiographical reflections with focus-group anecdotes from rural southeastern Ohio residents to illustrate two communication/narrative concepts—'liminality' and 'otherness'—in stories about living with water, Mother Nature, fracking, C8 river contamination, and transitioning from private wells/springs to township water. Although household water connection experiences are mentioned anecdotally (c1 = yes, c4 = yes), the paper does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing household water service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2 (c2 = no), and it lacks basic methodological reporting (sample size, number of focus groups, analytic method) and an identifiable governance exposure–outcome design (c5 = no).
